common_name: Big Bob Chinese Ground Orchid (Large-Flowered Robust Hardy Ground Orchid)

planting.note: Plant pseudobulbs or divisions in spring, just below the soil surface, in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade; Big Bob is a selection prized for notably larger pseudobulbs, broader foliage, and bigger magenta-pink flowers than the typical species.

directions: Big Bob is a robust, larger-growing selection of the Chinese ground orchid, chosen for its oversized pleated leaves and bigger, deeper magenta-pink flower spikes compared with the common species form. Grow it as you would the species: in humus-rich, evenly moist but well-drained soil in dappled shade, with a protective winter mulch of leaf litter in the colder end of its hardiness range to shield the shallow pseudobulbs from freeze-thaw damage. It is one of the more forgiving terrestrial orchids in cultivation, tolerating ordinary garden conditions and multiplying by offset pseudobulbs into a fuller, more imposing clump than standard Bletilla striata within a few seasons. Divide crowded clumps every three to four years in spring, just as new growth emerges, to maintain vigor and increase stock.
sources: Plant Delights Nursery / Juniper Level Botanic Garden

planting.note: Plant dormant, nursery-propagated bare-root crowns in fall just beneath the soil surface in humus-rich, well-drained but evenly moist woodland soil in partial shade; this is one of the European Cypripedium breeding program hybrids distributed through specialty laboratories, bred for improved vigor over wild species.

directions: Cypripedium 'Philipp' is a named garden hybrid from the German Cypripedium breeding program behind well-known selections such as 'Gisela' and 'Ulla Silkens', propagated by tissue culture and sold by specialty laboratories as a more garden-tolerant alternative to wild-collected lady's slippers. All hardy Cypripedium, hybrids included, depend on a specific mycorrhizal fungus in the root zone to take up nutrients, so success hinges on starting with lab-propagated, fungus-inoculated stock and leaving it completely undisturbed once planted rather than attempting to divide or transplant it. Site crowns in a cool, humus-rich woodland bed with dappled shade, sharp drainage, and steady moisture through the growing season, and mulch lightly with leaf litter each autumn to insulate the shallow roots. Even as a hybrid bred for easier cultivation, expect a slow, multi-year establishment period before plants bulk up into reliable, multi-stemmed flowering clumps.

planting.note: Transplant container-grown or nursery-propagated plants in spring into humus-rich, well-drained woodland soil in partial to full shade; this European native spreads readily by seed and rhizome once established and is considered weedy or locally invasive in parts of North America, so site it deliberately and monitor for unwanted spread.

directions: Broad-leaved helleborine is the easiest hardy terrestrial orchid to grow from this genus, producing leafy upright stems topped with loose spikes of small, drooping greenish flowers flushed purple or pink in mid to late summer, when few other woodland orchids are in bloom. Unlike most terrestrial orchids, it is not fussy about a narrow band of mycorrhizal partners and establishes readily in ordinary humus-rich woodland soil in dappled to fairly deep shade, tolerating a wide range of conditions once settled. Its ease of cultivation is a double-edged trait: in parts of North America, where it is an introduced species, it self-seeds and spreads by rhizome aggressively enough to be classed as weedy or locally invasive, so give it a contained spot and remove unwanted seedlings rather than letting it colonize a wild woodland edge. In its native European range it is a welcome, low-maintenance shade garden orchid that needs no winter protection and multiplies slowly into clumps without special care.
sources: USDA Natural Resources Conservation Service PLANTS Database
